principles.title: No self-confirmation
principles.text: Evidence a member gives about its own statement does not count. Only lines from others can support or oppose it.

principles.title: Support and opposition are separate
principles.text: What speaks for a statement and what speaks against it are recorded separately. Both can be present at the same time; neither cancels the other silently.

principles.title: Four values, absence only over a closed view
principles.text: A statement is true when there is support and, in a complete view of the evidence, no opposition; false when there is opposition and no support; both when there is support and opposition; unknown when a complete view shows neither. Without a complete view nothing is concluded from what is missing: missing evidence is never evidence against.

principles.title: Sufficient reason
principles.text: Every value names its reason: the lines of evidence behind it, or for the unknown the closed snapshot that was searched. A value without a reason is a violation.

principles.title: Acceptance needs independence
principles.text: A statement is accepted when at least two independent lines support it and none opposes it; with one line it is only a hypothesis. It is rejected when two independent lines oppose it. Conflicting or unknown statements stay unresolved. Two lines from the same origin are one line.

principles.title: Duties of a member
principles.text: A member may assert only what is accepted, and may state a hypothesis only as a hypothesis. It must not assert what is tentative, rejected or unresolved. It must report a conflict, and ask the collective about an unknown statement when another member offers knowledge about it. It never confirms its own statement and never adopts foreign knowledge before it is reviewed.

principles.title: External sources count only when proven
principles.text: A source outside the collective — a retrieval hit or a web page — is a source of truth like any other line of evidence, but only when the statement was verified against it: the passage that says it was found in the source. Then the source's reference is the reason, so the truth can always be shown. An unverified source counts for nothing; it must be verified and must not be cited. Two independent verified sources make a statement accepted, one makes it a hypothesis — the same reference twice is one source.
